links.summary: Subframe is a macOS design tool where "the canvas is based on HTML & React, so you can implement it exactly as designed" — open localhost or any website in built-in browser tabs, iterate live, and work with Claude Code and Codex "directly in Subframe" using your own subscription, or bring design context to external agents via the Subframe MCP. It's "a browser, for building": Free is $0/month (one project, unlimited viewers & editors, limited AI credits), Pro is $20/editor/month (unlimited projects, 6x AI credits), with AI credits consumed only in the web version or when used instead of your Claude / Codex subscription.

Complexity is never a conscious design goal, but "it arises inherently as new features are pursued or new components are introduced," and "over time, technologies are added, but are rarely removed" — so production minimalism means making simplicity an objective in itself. The aim is Buckminster Fuller's ephemeralization, "do more and more with less and less until eventually you can do everything with nothing": build a stack that scales to more users while the people and infrastructure supporting it stay fixed. In practice that means retiring old technology when new tech goes in, standardizing on one database, language, job queue and web server, avoiding custom software and favoring services — "It's not that new technology should *never* be introduced, but it should be done with rational defensiveness."

Koboyo is an infinite canvas where you "Pick a tool from here": Rectangle (R), ellipse (O), arrow (A), Slides & Diagrams as Code, zoom & reset view, and keyboard shortcuts. "Double-click anywhere to add text or pick a tool."

Small, sharp tools — "minimalist, composable programs that worked in concert to a degree of effectiveness that was more than the sum of their parts" — come from Unix and "lent itself quite naturally to building modern web platforms," which is why the idea carries over to service-oriented architecture and microservices. The catch is Raymond's Rule of Minimality: "Choose the shared context you want to manage, and build your programs as small as those boundaries will allow," because "Small, sharp tools in the Unix style have trouble sharing data, unless they live inside a framework that makes communication among them easy" — a tool can be too large *or* too small. At Heroku they got it wrong with a separate organization service whose private API surface "swelled to an unmanageable size," and re-integrating it beat the two services kept apart: "the sum of their complexity was much greater than that of the integrated system."

This is just the acknowledgments page for Andy Grove's book, thanking his patient family, Matthew Powers for inspiring him to write it, and "the countless people who have interacted with me over the past six years as I worked on the DataFusion project." It notes the book is "also available for purchase in ePub, MOBI, and PDF format from https://leanpub.com/how-query-engines-work" — because it's an acknowledgments page, there is no teaching, table of contents, FAQ, or pricing beyond that Leanpub pointer. Honestly, it's thin.

Tripwire is "the firewall for your OSS projects" — install the GitHub App and it ingests contributor activity, then runs every change request through workflows of triggers, rules, gates and actions so you can "Block noise. Pass signal." Rules screen on account age, rate limits, hidden links and max files changed, org members are exempt, and every run keeps its evidence, with "One comment. One check. Zero noise." It's not priced on the page — you "Request access" and "Join the beta," with "Request an invite" for custom workflows.

dither-kit is dithered charts & components for shadcn/ui — install via @dither-kit/cli ("lockfile for update / diff, pulls core + deps automatically") or paste into Claude Code, Cursor, or any agent to install + wire up a chart, and files land in components/dither-kit/. Charts are tweakable from the floating dial panel with knobs like `variant`, `bloom`, `stackType`, `colors`, `animate`, and `interactive`, and the standalone button and gradient don't pull in the chart engine.

celld is a self-hosted version of the Durable Objects model: Workers handle requests while Durable Objects, KV, Queues, D1, and Workflows keep their state in cells, each with its own SQLite database, and the fleet needs "no membership protocol, failure detector, or consensus service." It's for anyone who wants the model with control over where cells run, how their state is stored, and how they investigate failures — "a primitive this good deserves to run anywhere." V8 + SQLite + LTX: "A stateful distributed system built on S3."

Netlify was emailing every new user with a personalized, plainly designed offer to help, and the email had a reply rate of just 1% — "they were missing a huge opportunity by failing to reach 99 of every 100 users." Cutting the text by 75% (150+ words to 37) raised replies to 4%, and cutting another 50% (to 14 words) doubled it again to 8% — length cut 90%, reply rates up 700%, and "that's the power of saying less." The advice: take your welcome email, cut anything unnecessary, take out another 50%, and A/B test positive replies against the original.

MotherDuck is "the cloud data warehouse built on DuckDB" — "fast, serverless analytics powered by DuckDB — with dedicated compute for every user and every agent." Its agent-first architecture gives "an isolated compute instance for every person, dashboard, and agent," a Duckling spun up in milliseconds with cold starts under 100ms, plus Flights, Guides, and Dives for pipelines, agent context, and visualizations. No pricing or free tier appears on the page; it offers a Book a Demo or you can "start with your coding agent."

HTTP.DEV teaches that HTTP is "the foundation of data exchange on the web," walking through the request-response model (methods, URLs, headers, status codes), the versions from the original early-1990s spec through HTTP/1.0, 1.1, 2, and 3 with QUIC, and three core building blocks: headers, methods, status codes. Its security section covers HTTPS, HSTS, CORS, CSP, session cookies, and authentication, followed by a long See also index of linked topics. There's no FAQ, no pricing, and nothing thin here — just the protocol, explained.

Lisse is a small JavaScript library that draws squircle corners, "the same continuous curve Figma and iOS use," with bindings for React, Vue, and Svelte plus a framework-agnostic core. Per-corner control, borders, and shadows are included, and the live demo shows "how far the squircle pulls in from the CSS-rounded back."

"Kimaki turns Discord into the control surface for your coding agents" — a collaborative agent orchestrator that connects to OpenCode, where "channels are projects" and "threads are sessions." You run `npx -y kimaki@latest`, the CLI walks you through setup in about a minute, and the source is on GitHub; Kimaki checks Discord permissions before processing any message and can use your existing Claude Pro/Max and ChatGPT/Codex subscriptions instead of paying per token.

The smarter you are, the stronger your conviction, the bigger the gap between what you say about your product and what people presently want — so stop saying what people already have, what you've built, or what you fantasize about, and just **say something people want**. Throw the old positioning playbooks in the trash: a months-long conference-room debate that produces "bullshit consensus" like "the OS for the unstructured data security fabric" has zero chance now, when Slack, Wiz, Cloudflare, Fin, and Harvey all win by becoming known for *doing* something rather than *being* something. Define the people, invite 30 of them to chat, and pull out their aspiration, desired outcome, and requirements — Kumo got data scientists excited with "move from predictive modeling to predictive AI," not with graph transformers.

mamuso is manuel muñoz solera, "a designer from Villena, Alicante, based in beautiful California, building fun things at SpaceXAI," whose longest-running hobby is photography with guitar a close second. Under "Having fun" he lists UnicodeKit ("Browsing characters like it's 1988"), Stray characters, Papercups, a Figma Orgchart plugin ("I promise I'm fun at parties"), and GitHub Actions including Discussion → Markdown, Weekly Update, Figma → Website ("Should designers code?"), Close Figma Tabs and Unvlogable. There's also a feed of notes running from "Design advice from Bill Hader" to "A little bit of character."

boat is "the cheapest, most powerful sandbox for agents, built for agent factories" — a sandbox being a persistent Ubuntu VM with SSH and SCP access, Docker support inside the VM, a dedicated IPv6 or IPv4 per machine, a 60fps virtual desktop, and fast disk-level forking from a snapshot, "built for AI agents, for programmatic use, and for humans." Pricing is "simple, honest pricing": pay only for the sandboxes you run, billed by the second, with a $20 minimum per month ($20 buys 2,000,000 VM-seconds, about 555 hours, of dedicated 4 vCPU / 8 GB VM-time, spread across one sandbox or many), a 7-day free trial with 25 compute hours, and boat claims to be "the most affordable option compared with E2B, Daytona, Modal, Vercel Sandbox, Railway, and others." Bring any agent: Claude Code, Codex, or OpenCode.

Being good at building and being good at shipping are two separate skills, and in the short term they're actually countervailing: if you have a gift for building, you're likely to be *worse* at shipping. Gifted programmers freeze up rather than ship flawed code, and writers hold back drafts that don't match their taste — but "you have to bias towards shipping", because you "can't improve *no* diff" and you can't predict what people will find interesting or useful. "You have to be momentum-based, not outcome-based. In other words, you have to grit your teeth and ship it."

Highlighters is a library that lets you draw marker strokes over web text — "not a coloured box sitting behind the words, an actual stroke off a nib: ink that pools where a line starts and stops, streaks left behind as it dries, a little bleed past the last letter." There are three nibs (broad chisel, rounded bullet, fine point), marks are painted on top so words stay selectable and searchable and hold their place through scrolling and resize, and overlapping passes darken like two real ones. It's small, runs anywhere, and ships with bindings for React, Vue and Svelte: npm install @highlighters/core.

Thorsten Ball plants his flag on what he believed in September 2026: "Code review will die," unit tests might die too, and "the craft of writing code will disappear" while "the craft of building software will be more important than ever." Most bugs become "you asked for the wrong thing" bugs, open source's eyeballs are now artificial, the terminal goes arcane like Perl one-liners, and tokens become "the new computing paradigm" — post-binary, with PM/Design/Eng, Agile, and SCRUM dead, UI generated on the fly, and some people priced out for lack of tokens. It'll take a generation to play out, but: "But do you want to have that job?"

Jan is "Your personal intelligence. Run any model, your way." It’s presented as an "Open-Source ChatGPT Replacement" that is "Free & Open source," with 6.9M+ downloads and "built in public" for the people who build and use it.

The senior engineer death spiral: you take a new job or a big project, decide to "cosplay being a more senior engineer than you are," disappear for weeks, give the "positive update," then tell yourself you'll do a whole month's work in a week and no one will know — until you burn out, get PIP'd, or quit. The fix is counterintuitive: assume everyone is operating in good faith, drop a level and be the greatest teammate for a while (bugs, grunt work, write-ups), because "you want to move away from an outcome-based mindset to momentum-based." Remember, "you are in the reputation-building business, and software is actually downstream of that" — big projects aren't done with big efforts, just slow, steady, incremental work.

“Your agent, in any app. Type @@ to ask your agent in any text field.” AtAt is a Mac app that lets you ask your agent in any editable text field and has TabTab complete your next words right where you type, with history, clipboard data, and settings staying on your Mac by default (optional iCloud Sync is off until you enable it). It needs an Apple silicon Mac on macOS 15+, and starts with 7 days free — no account or payment card — then $59 yearly or $169 lifetime, both with a 30-day refund promise.

Knap turns data into Markdown: "Add variables inline with Markdown. Filters modify values and formatting." You generate Markdown from Knap templates with `npx knap render template.md --data data.json --output note.md`, or add Knap templating to your app via `npm install knap`. It also points to the Obsidian Web Clipper to "Save web pages to Markdown with customizable templates."

Cactus is on-device AI for "mobile, wearables, AR glasses, smart homes, robots, cars, Macs/PCs, game consoles, TVs, microcontrollers" — 2-bit, 8-29MB, runs locally, up to 4k tokens/sec decode speed, backed by Y Combinator. Pebble founder Eric Migicovsky says of Cactus Needle: "We run Cactus Needle locally in the app, instead of relying on the cloud. The model's footprint is tiny and the performance never lets us down."

Scritto is a JavaScript library that animates text in place: give an element a new value and "only the characters that changed move: each one rolls from the old character to the new one while the rest hold their position." It works on numbers, words, and emoji, with bindings for React, Vue, Svelte, and Solid, and a core that runs without a framework — and the page counts its own visitors, opens, pokes, and downloads up as they happen.

Expertise comes from applied friction — "you have to fail to succeed" — but AI coding tools demand expertise while actively circumventing the friction that cultivates it, so novices leaning on generation skip crucial planning stages and finish with an "illusion of competence" rather than true understanding. The prescription is to "largely disregard the pure code generation capabilities of these models" and use them as Socratic sparring partners, interactive documentation, and dynamic tutorial generators, since "the most productive learning that can happen with an AI coding tool is when it isn't used to generate much of any code at all."

hilos is "a team chat where agents are members" — ask for a change in a channel and agents ship real PRs, other agents review, people approve. It's free, and agents run on your machine, on your own account.

I am obsessed with smooth corners — squircles — and "CSS gave me a radius and nothing else, and no browser drew a real curve." So I built Lisse: no superellipse, no approximation, a Bézier eased into an arc, faithful to the corner as Apple renders one, taking a radius and a smoothing value per corner, reading the border and shadow you already wrote and redrawing them as SVG with inner shadows included, and caching solved corners so five thousand identical corners cost about what fifty do. It ships with a site at corne.rs where the headword plays one of six recordings and drops loose with real physics, plus Chrome and Firefox extensions to enforce my love of smooth corners on every website I visit. It is early, open source, MIT, and I would like people to pull it apart and tell me where it breaks.

Okara is "the only AI CMO you need for growth and marketing," with "10+ Marketing Agents Running 24/7" that first research and prepare strategy documents — product-information.md, marketing-strategy.md, competitor-analysis.md, brand-voice.md, content-strategy.md — then execute channel by channel: influencer, Reddit, SEO, writer, X, LinkedIn, GEO, coding, and UGC video agents. Connect WordPress, Webflow, Framer, Wix, Sanity, Search Console, Analytics, GitHub, LinkedIn, X, TikTok, Instagram, WhatsApp, Telegram, or Slack once, and approved work publishes and reports back automatically. It's "Free to start · No credit card required," used by 100,000+ users, and pitches "The $14,000/mo job from $129/mo."

Equals is "a single source of truth for the entire team. Same question? Same answer." You build dashboards and models in a spreadsheet calculation layer, then deploy them — a scheduled Slack push, calculated values into your CRM, live charts in Notion — because "all your GTM data synced and cleaned in a Snowflake instance we run for you," and any agent connects over MCP to analyze "the metrics your team trusts—not numbers it invented."

Wellmade is "A home for well made creative work." The homepage unfolds as a stream of pieces from individual makers and studios — a video with a poster frame, "All In", an "early identity concept", and "brand identity for pera" — each credited to its creator. A visitor gets the work itself: the image, the video, and whose hands made it.

Finding problems worth solving isn't separate from the rest of the job: instead of staring at a blank page trying to "think strategically," I act like a sponge — absorbing problems rather than requests, letting them accumulate until the same issue pops up in different teams or several awkward requests "collapse into a single idea." The caution is that "a common shape is only a hypothesis and elegance is not evidence," so ideas get pressure-tested with throwaway prototypes or dropped outright before any real build. And solving useful problems feeds the next one: people come to me earlier, I see more of the org, and that trust lets me influence the roadmap without owning every project.

Building agents is still messy: "SDK abstractions break once you hit real tool use," and after adopting the Vercel AI SDK's provider abstractions and driving the loop himself, "we would not make that choice again" — explicit Anthropic-style cache management, provider-side tools, and clearer errors all argue for staying on the raw platform SDKs. Reinforcement in the loop "ends up doing more heavy lifting than expected" (the todo write tool is basically "just an echo tool"), failures need isolating in subagents, and a virtual file system is what keeps image generation, code execution and RunInference from becoming dead ends. Output tooling is "surprisingly tricky," model choice still depends on the task — Haiku and Sonnet remain "the best tool callers available" while Gemini 2.5 handles summarization, PDFs and images — and testing and evals are "the hardest problem here," with nothing yet making him happy.

effect-mq is "Effect-native" job queueing where "Jobs are schemas, handlers are Effects, workers are Layers" — interruption, retries, and timeouts run on the Effect runtime "instead of bolted-on process machinery." Storage is a seam ("Postgres through your drizzle schema, Redis through atomic Lua scripts, memory for tests"), with a producer/runner split enforced by the type system so you "Ship producers in your API and runners on separate machines," plus a run ledger, repeatable schedules, dedup modes, cancellation, tracing and metrics. Install is `bun add effect-mq` (or npm / pnpm / yarn).

Learn Inference bills itself as "an interactive companion to *Inference Engineering* by Philip Kiely" — it "follows the book's structure and covers the same ground," with rewritten explanations and simulators "for the parts you grasp faster by turning a dial than by reading a paragraph." The pitch is that "Training teaches a model what it knows. Inference is everything that happens afterward, every time somebody uses it, and it is where the bill actually lands," spanning "attention kernels at one end, GPU procurement across three clouds at the other." The page itself is still thin: one demo from chapter 1 (Figure 1.4, time to first token versus tokens per second, with "illustrative numbers") and a Chapters list holding only a Glossary so far.

Modem "discovers and organizes your customer concerns" — it reads support threads, sales calls, community posts and social comments, works out who raised what, then groups every mention of the same problem into one topic linked to the issues and PRs fixing it, so product, engineering, success and sales work from the same record. The pitch is "Less digging, more shipping": product research drops from 3–4 hours to 10 minutes, and "agents read Modem's context graph vs the raw threads underneath" for 98% fewer tokens. Pricing starts at Free ($0/mo, 2,500 events + limited agent usage), then Startup $80/mo and Scale $250/mo — unlimited users on every plan, Scale free for 14 days, Enterprise custom.

Delta is "a multiplayer environment for coding with agents" where the unit of work is a thread — the conversation with an agent and the checkout of the repository it works in, kept together as one shareable artifact you can invite teammates into, review in context, and open from desktop, web, or a cloud runner. Underneath it, DeltaDB is the version control layer: where Git captures a snapshot at each commit, DeltaDB "records work as a stream of fine-grained deltas," each with a stable identity so a reference anchors to a change rather than a line number. Early adopters put it as "Git remembers the commit. This remembers everything between them, including the conversation that wrote the code."
This page is "Learn Harness Engineering" — it renders only a title and a "Skip to content" link while the rest is still "Loading...". Beyond that heading, nothing is on the page yet.

Models.dev is "an open-source database of AI models," laid out as one long table of Model, Lab, Providers, Context, Output, Reasoning, Tool Call, Structured, Temperature, Weights, Price, Release and Updated. Each row links to a model page — and to Hugging Face for weights marked Open — spanning labs from Anthropic and OpenAI to Zhipu AI, DeepSeek, Xiaomi and MiniMax, with prices like $0.10 / $0.50 or $0.00 / $0.00 shown per model.

Rather than remembering "a few clunky incantations" for every repo — `rust fmt`? `./gradlew build` or `mvn`? `yarn` or `npm` or `pnpm`? — the author builds convenience tooling so he can just say "build the code", "lint it", "format it", "install dependencies", applying muscle memory across repositories "no matter the repository I'm in". He walks through four ways to do it: a simple bash script (`run build`, `run test`), `make` with `.PHONY` targets and tab autocompletion, `just` (Make's familiar look minus the weirder parts), and `mise` with its `mise.toml` tasks. "This is not exactly rocket science" — a small quality of life improvement for you and your team that's "super simple to set up and yet it's something I rarely see in the wild".

The Pudding publishes "Visual Data Stories About Just About Everything" — numbered entries like #225 "life after death?" ("A room of thousands of humans wrestling with what comes after it all"), #224 "mowing experiment," and #199 "middle school sucks." The run is dated by month and year from #225 (Oct 2026) back to #199 (Mar 2025), mixing interactive analyses ("An analysis of 200,000 similes from popular fiction") with video ("A six-minute video about the loneliness epidemic, in data"). "Get The Pudding in your inbox," and "If you like our stories, you'll love our merch" — "Shop our swag."

Wondering is "Duolingo for learning anything" — it turns a topic like LLMs, quantum mechanics, or product design into a structured course of three-minute lessons you can "watch a narrated video, listen to it as a podcast, or read it with diagrams and visuals." The page lays out the pitch ("A better habit than doomscrolling"), the gamification (daily streaks, friend streaks, XP, streak freezes), a "How Wondering works" list (bite-sized lessons, spaced repetition with the FSRS algorithm, personalization, an AI tutor), and "Start learning" links to public courses, a job-focused AI course, Canvas, comparisons, and the iPhone app. There's no pricing and no FAQ here — it's a landing page, not a deep one.

A study my colleagues and I conducted used Britain's postwar sugar rationing — which ended in September 1953, when consumption nearly doubled — to ask whether how much sugar you consumed before your second birthday shapes your health into your 70s. Among over 64,000 people born in Britain between 1951 and 1956, those who spent longer under rationing during their first 1,000 days had lower incidence of five cancers (liver cancer rates around 69% lower, breast 36% lower) and longer telomeres, "equivalent to about 2.2 years of slower biological ageing." What's most surprising is that early-life sugar exposure "continued to affect people's diets even 50 years later" — they still consumed less sugar in adulthood, around age 50.

Agents do the heavy lifting of understanding and changing source now, so the expense of personalizing software has dropped dramatically — software that can be personalized "doesn't need a plugin system or a config file," just a prompt and a nightly cron job rebasing local changes on upstream. Whole categories of products "need to be reinvented" for single users and small teams, and where Claude Code is closed-source, "you don't get to personalize it" — "the source code is the extension system."

pgbot is Postgres intelligence for AI agents & apps: 'Nobody reads database metrics. pgbot does.' Connect your Postgres and 'Get answers, not dashboards: what's healthy, what's broken, and what to fix first' for any cloud via direct access or an agent that never leaves your network. It also speaks MCP as a read-only tool exposing inspect and unused_indexes, and its agent is open-source with read-only access for secure production use.

The LLM Inference Handbook is "your technical glossary, guidebook, and reference - all in one," covering everything from core concepts and performance metrics like Time to First Token and Tokens per Second to optimization techniques (continuous batching, prefix caching), GPU architecture, and deployment patterns like BYOC and on-prem. It was written because "LLM inference knowledge is often fragmented" and much of it "assumes you already understand half the stack," so it targets engineers deploying, scaling or operating LLMs in production, whether fine-tuning a small open model or running large-scale deployments. It is built for learning by trying, with interactive tools including a LLM Inference Visualizer, GPU Memory Calculator, Batching Strategy Simulator, Warp Scheduler Visualizer and Kernel Fusion Visualizer, and it is "continuously updated with the latest best practices and field-tested insights."

The future worth building is human — shaped by human knowledge, guided by human will, and decided by human judgment — because productive knowledge is tacit, local, fleeting, and held privately, so "central planning fails not because of insufficient intelligence, but because of the nature of productive knowledge." So Thinking Machines trains strong models, builds tools that let people fine-tune models with their own knowledge, and makes a long-term bet on interaction models that handle live, multimodal interaction natively, treating "participation vs. capability, ownership vs. safe alignment" as technical challenges rather than trade-offs. Alignment becomes "a feature not of a single model but of an ecosystem of AIs raised in different places, disagreeing, competing, and learning from each other" — keeping the weirdness alive.

treg is "the tool catalog for your agent" — one command into Claude Code hands it "the catalog · 3,900+ endpoints · one key" across 111 providers, choosing by what treg has measured ("success rate, speed, last time it answered") rather than a guess. It's "No subscription, pay for results": price shown before the call, fractions of a cent per call, $1.00 free to start, and "your own key always wins" — bring a provider key and those calls route through it, unmetered. It's "100% open source · AGPL" with "0% additional fee," and if you're "Building an API or a skill worth sharing? List your tool in the catalog."

Iris is "A camera for coding agents" — "One fast command or MCP tool call produces one trustworthy image," rendered with your real installed Chrome over the DevTools Protocol, with a local stdio MCP server in the same binary exposing one `capture` tool. Install with `curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/brijr/iris/main/install.sh | sh` or `cargo install iris-screenshot` (the crates.io package is named iris-screenshot; the installed command is iris), and the only runtime dependency is an installed Chrome-family browser. Licensed MIT, and "Batch capture, browser interaction scripting, diffs, and review workflows remain outside Iris."

Nautilus is “Science Connected,” publishing headlines like “A Distant Planet Emitted a Burst of Radio Waves. Why?” and “The Secret Superpowers of Amphibians and Reptiles,” alongside Latest Stories and a new print issue, The Stupid Issue. This page doesn’t name editors or writers, and it lists no cadence or subscription details.

Feather is a tool with a Brief that "removes what's done, keep what matters, and nudges what needs you," plus Sorting — "an inbox that sorts, merges, and surfaces insights, on its own." The page shows no pricing, free tier, or open-source status.

Ankur Sethi still uses coding assistants on personal projects, but letting them "roam free" leaves him with "a colossal amount of cognitive debt," and reviewing AI-generated PRs is not fun — "personal projects must be fun above all else." His fix is grossly inefficient and slightly comical: agents files instruct the LLM to never touch project files and instead show every proposed edit in chat so he can type it in manually, trading 10x speed for about 2x, and building a mental model and spatial map of his codebase while catching hallucinations and bad design as he goes. It's the same lesson as being told never to copy-paste code as a teenager: "I value comprehension over productivity," because the industry is taking on cognitive debt it will have to pay back soon.

Hatchet is "the orchestration engine for teams who ship" — "Write tasks and workflows as code" with native SDKs in TypeScript, Python, and Go, run workers on your own cloud, and use the orchestration engine as "a managed service or can be self-hosted." It's "Fully MIT-licensed" with "Running Hatchet locally... a single CLI command away," covering background tasks, durable tasks, DAGs, cron jobs, retries, rate limits, priorities, OpenTelemetry, and Prometheus metrics, for use cases like AI agents, data ingestion, and webhooks. "There are two components to running Hatchet: the orchestration engine and your workers."

30,954 people mowed the same lawn and found 14,589 different ways to do it, but the median person still hit 91% efficiency and 16% did it perfectly. Unlike the Traveling Salesman Problem, where humans get worse as problems grow, optimality held around 90% whether the lawn took 26 moves or 177, which suggests "layout matters more than raw size." What separated the best mowers came down to a single critical decision — mowing the right side first so they could end on the left and dodge the dead-end trap — because "it's not about thinking more or faster, but *when* thinking happens."

Articles is a directory of pieces like “Natural language as source code, conventional code as a build artifact” and “A natural filter for bad ideas.” It points to writing on AI, design engineering, gradients, agents, and Postgres.

Artificial Analysis is "Independent analysis of AI" — an Intelligence Index, Coding Agent Index, Cyber Index, plus cost, speed, latency and provider comparisons, so you can "Understand the AI landscape to choose the best model and provider for your use case." Benchmarks include AA-Briefcase, GDPval-AA, AA-Omniscience, Terminal-Bench 4.0, Harvey LAB-AA and others, alongside Image, Video, Text to Image and Speech arenas, with new model evaluations and articles tracked in a changelog. Many figures on the page render as "Not publicly available."

Break down CSS backgrounds, layer by layer: paste any background CSS and see what each layer contributes — separately. The playground shows each radial, conic, or linear layer in a draggable list you can reorder, or you can try an example.

Pullfrog is a GitHub bot that runs AI agents on your repo: it "listens for GitHub events—PRs opened, issues created, reviews submitted, CI failures—and triggers agent runs based on your configuration," or you can "tag `@pullfrog` for anything ad-hoc." It's open source with "No per-seat pricing" — "Personal accounts and public repositories stay free" under the Developer plan, Organization is $30/month, Enterprise is custom, with a 14-day trial and no card required. Runs happen in your repo's GitHub Actions, with your own keys or the "Claude/Codex/Grok/Kimi/OpenCode plans" you already pay for.

A border-radius is just a number, but roundness is relative — "The same 12px looks generous on a small button and almost flat on a wide card" — and nested corners need a shared center, so the inner radius is the outer radius minus the full gap, border counted as gap. Tokens give you the scale and do nothing for the rule, so a system should "write the relationship, not the result": hold onto the formula, not the number it happens to produce, then let your eye take it the final pixel or two. It works because the default corner is a quarter circle, and with `corner-shape` and squircles subtraction no longer nests cleanly — "The formula was always a floor, not a finish. Squircles take the floor away."
